entities.name: Salmon
entities.fact: Salmon hatch in rivers, grow fat at sea, and find their way back to the very stream where they were born, guided partly by smell.

entities.name: Trout
entities.fact: Several trout, including brown and rainbow trout, have sea-run forms that feed in the ocean and return to rivers to spawn.

entities.name: Atlantic salmon
entities.fact: Atlantic salmon return from the sea to the river where they hatched, and unlike Pacific salmon some survive spawning and go back to sea to spawn again.

entities.name: Chinook salmon
entities.fact: The chinook, or king salmon, is the largest Pacific salmon and some swim about 3,000 kilometres up the Yukon River to spawn.

entities.name: Sockeye salmon
entities.fact: Sockeye salmon turn brilliant red with green heads when they return from the sea to spawn, and landlocked populations are known as kokanee.

entities.name: Coho salmon
entities.fact: Coho, or silver salmon, spend about a year in fresh water and roughly 18 months at sea before returning to spawn with hooked jaws and red flanks.

entities.name: Pink salmon
entities.fact: Pink salmon are the smallest and most abundant Pacific salmon and live on a strict two-year cycle, so odd-year and even-year runs never mix.

entities.name: Chum salmon
entities.fact: Chum salmon have the widest range of any Pacific salmon, from California to Korea, and spawning males develop tiger-like purple stripes.

entities.name: Masu salmon
entities.fact: The masu or cherry salmon is the Pacific salmon of Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East, and some populations never leave their rivers.

entities.name: Rainbow trout
entities.fact: Rainbow trout that migrate to sea are called steelhead; they return silver and powerful to spawn in their home rivers and can spawn more than once.

entities.name: Brown trout
entities.fact: Brown trout that migrate to sea come back silver and much larger, and are then known as sea trout.

entities.name: Cutthroat trout
entities.fact: Cutthroat trout are named for the red slash under the jaw, and coastal populations migrate down to the sea and back.

entities.name: Brook trout
entities.fact: The brook trout is actually a char, with light spots on a dark background, and is the official state fish of several US states.

entities.name: Lake trout
entities.fact: Lake trout are big, slow-growing char of cold northern lakes that can live for more than 25 years.

entities.name: Bull trout
entities.fact: The bull trout is a char of cold, clean rivers in north-west North America and is so sensitive to warm water that it is listed as threatened.

entities.name: Dolly Varden
entities.fact: The Dolly Varden is a char named after a brightly dressed character in a Charles Dickens novel, and many populations migrate to sea and back.

entities.name: Arctic char
entities.fact: The Arctic char lives further north than any other freshwater fish, and sea-run char return to rivers each autumn to spawn.

entities.name: Golden trout
entities.fact: The golden trout, with its brilliant gold and red colours, lives in the high Sierra Nevada and is the state freshwater fish of California.

entities.name: Apache trout
entities.fact: The Apache trout is found only in the White Mountains of Arizona and is the official state fish of Arizona.

entities.name: Gila trout
entities.fact: The Gila trout survives in a handful of mountain streams in New Mexico and Arizona and was among the first fish listed as endangered in the United States.

entities.name: Marble trout
entities.fact: The marble trout of Slovenia and northern Italy has a marbled pattern instead of spots and can grow to well over a metre long.

entities.name: Huchen
entities.fact: The huchen, or Danube salmon, is a giant trout relative of the Danube basin that can grow to more than a metre long and never goes to sea.

entities.name: Taimen
entities.fact: The taimen of Siberia and Mongolia is the largest salmonid in the world, reaching about 2 metres and living for more than 50 years.

entities.name: Sakhalin taimen
entities.fact: The Sakhalin taimen of Japan and the Russian Far East is a critically endangered giant that migrates between rivers and the sea.

entities.name: Lenok
entities.fact: The lenok, sometimes called the Asiatic trout, lives in the cold rivers of Siberia, Mongolia, China and Korea.

entities.name: Sevan trout
entities.fact: The Sevan trout is found naturally only in Lake Sevan in Armenia and is endangered after the lake was lowered for irrigation and power.

entities.name: Ohrid trout
entities.fact: The Ohrid trout lives only in Lake Ohrid, one of the oldest lakes in Europe, on the border of North Macedonia and Albania.

entities.name: Adriatic trout
entities.fact: The Adriatic, or softmouth, trout of the Balkans has a soft fleshy snout unlike any other trout and lives in a few rivers draining to the Adriatic.

entities.name: Mexican golden trout
entities.fact: The Mexican golden trout lives in mountain streams of the Sierra Madre Occidental and is the southernmost native trout in North America.

entities.name: Lahontan cutthroat trout
entities.fact: The Lahontan cutthroat is the largest subspecies of cutthroat trout, native to Nevada's Pyramid Lake, and is the state fish of Nevada.

entities.name: Eel
entities.fact: Freshwater eels hatch in the open ocean, spend years growing in rivers and lakes, and then return to the sea to spawn and die.

entities.name: European eel
entities.fact: The European eel can spend 20 years or more in rivers before swimming about 5,000 kilometres to spawn in the Sargasso Sea.

entities.name: American eel
entities.fact: The American eel grows up in rivers from Greenland to Brazil and returns to the Sargasso Sea to spawn, like its European cousin.

entities.name: Japanese eel
entities.fact: The Japanese eel, the unagi of Japanese cooking, spawns near the Mariana Islands and its young drift thousands of kilometres back to East Asian rivers.

entities.name: Sturgeon
entities.fact: Most sturgeons spend their adult lives in the sea or in large lakes and swim up rivers to spawn, and some live for more than 100 years.

entities.name: Atlantic sturgeon
entities.fact: The Atlantic sturgeon lives in coastal seas and swims up rivers to spawn, and in the past grew to more than 4 metres long.

entities.name: Striped bass
entities.fact: Striped bass spawn in rivers such as the Hudson and the tributaries of Chesapeake Bay and spend their adult lives roaming the Atlantic coast.

entities.name: American shad
entities.fact: American shad live at sea and surge up east-coast rivers each spring to spawn, a run so huge it once fed George Washington's troops at Valley Forge.

entities.name: Alewife
entities.fact: The alewife is a small herring that migrates from the sea into rivers to spawn, and landlocked populations invaded the Great Lakes through canals.

entities.name: Rainbow smelt
entities.fact: Rainbow smelt live in coastal seas and run up rivers to spawn in early spring, and freshly caught smelt smell faintly of cucumber.

entities.name: Striped mullet
entities.fact: Striped mullet wander freely between the sea, estuaries and completely fresh water, but spawn offshore in the open sea.

entities.name: Tarpon
entities.fact: Tarpon gulp air into a swim bladder that works like a lung, and young tarpon grow up in brackish and freshwater backwaters before moving out to sea.

entities.name: Common snook
entities.fact: Common snook spawn in salt water near inlets, and the young grow up in brackish creeks and freshwater rivers before moving back to the coast.

entities.name: Barramundi
entities.fact: Barramundi hatch in estuaries, grow up in fresh water and return to the sea to spawn, with most starting life as males and later changing into females.

entities.name: Sea lamprey
entities.fact: The sea lamprey grows up at sea clamped onto fish, rasping through their skin to feed on blood, then swims up rivers to spawn and die.

entities.name: Hilsa
entities.fact: The hilsa is a shad that lives in the Bay of Bengal and swims up the Ganges and other rivers to spawn, and it is the national fish of Bangladesh.

entities.name: Ayu
entities.fact: The ayu, or sweetfish, hatches in Japanese rivers, spends the winter at sea, and returns to the river to graze algae from the rocks.

entities.name: Eulachon
entities.fact: The eulachon is a small smelt so oily that a dried fish can be lit like a candle, and it runs from the sea up Pacific north-west rivers each spring.

entities.name: European flounder
entities.fact: The European flounder spawns at sea but often swims far up rivers into completely fresh water to feed.

entities.name: Three-spined stickleback
entities.fact: Many three-spined sticklebacks live at sea and move into fresh water to breed, where the red-bellied male builds a nest and guards the eggs.

entities.name: Inanga
entities.fact: The inanga of New Zealand and Australia lays its eggs on grasses flooded by spring tides, and the larvae are swept out to sea before returning as whitebait.

entities.name: Bull shark
entities.fact: Bull sharks can live in fresh water and have been found far up the Amazon and Mississippi rivers, and their young grow up in rivers and estuaries.

entities.name: Lungfish
entities.fact: Lungfish have true lungs as well as gills and are the closest living fish relatives of land animals.

entities.name: Mudskipper
entities.fact: Mudskippers spend much of their time out of water on mudflats, breathing through their skin and the lining of their mouth and throat.

entities.name: Betta
entities.fact: Bettas have a labyrinth organ above the gills that lets them gulp air at the surface, which is why they survive in still, oxygen-poor water.

entities.name: Snakehead
entities.fact: Snakeheads breathe air with a chamber above their gills and can wriggle short distances over land between ponds.

entities.name: Walking catfish
entities.fact: The walking catfish can breathe air and wriggle across land between ponds, which helped it spread as an invasive species in Florida.

entities.name: Arapaima
entities.fact: The arapaima of the Amazon must rise to gulp air every few minutes and can grow to about 3 metres long.

entities.name: Gourami
entities.fact: Gouramis have a labyrinth organ that lets them breathe air from the surface, so they thrive in warm, stagnant water.

entities.name: Gar
entities.fact: Gars can gulp air into a lung-like swim bladder, letting them survive in warm, stagnant water with little oxygen.

entities.name: Bowfin
entities.fact: The bowfin can breathe air using its swim bladder and is the only living member of a lineage dating back to the age of dinosaurs.

entities.name: Bichir
entities.fact: Bichirs have paired lungs and can breathe air, and young bichirs even have external gills like a salamander larva.

entities.name: Climbing perch
entities.fact: The climbing perch breathes air and can travel over land between ponds, pulling itself along with its gill covers and fins.

entities.name: Australian lungfish
entities.fact: The Australian lungfish has a single lung and surfaces to gulp air when its river water runs low in oxygen.

entities.name: African lungfish
entities.fact: African lungfish can survive months of drought buried in the mud inside a cocoon of dried mucus, breathing air through a small opening.

entities.name: Alligator gar
entities.fact: The alligator gar can grow well over 2 metres long and gulps air at the surface through a swim bladder that works like a lung.

entities.name: South American lungfish
entities.fact: The South American lungfish breathes mostly with its two lungs and digs a burrow in the mud when its swamp dries out.

entities.name: Longnose gar
entities.fact: The longnose gar gulps air at the surface and has a long, narrow snout filled with needle-like teeth.

entities.name: Weather loach
entities.fact: The weather loach swallows air and absorbs the oxygen through its gut, and is said to grow restless when air pressure drops before a storm.

entities.name: Swamp eel
entities.fact: The Asian swamp eel breathes air through the lining of its mouth and throat and can cross wet ground between ponds.

entities.name: Arowana
entities.fact: Arowanas can breathe air using their swim bladder and are famous for leaping out of the water to snatch insects from overhanging branches.

entities.name: Pleco
entities.fact: Plecos gulp air at the surface and absorb the oxygen through their stomach lining when the water runs low in oxygen.

entities.name: Giant gourami
entities.fact: The giant gourami can grow to about 70 centimetres and uses a labyrinth organ to breathe air.

entities.name: Northern snakehead
entities.fact: The northern snakehead can survive for days out of water if kept moist and has become an invasive species in North America.

entities.name: Dwarf gourami
entities.fact: The dwarf gourami breathes air with a labyrinth organ, and the male builds a floating nest of bubbles for the eggs.

entities.name: Ropefish
entities.fact: The ropefish has lungs as well as gills and can survive for a while out of water, slithering along like a snake.

entities.name: Senegal bichir
entities.fact: The Senegal bichir has paired lungs and is sometimes sold in aquariums as the dinosaur eel for its ancient look.

entities.name: Corydoras
entities.fact: Corydoras catfish dart to the surface to gulp air and absorb the oxygen through the lining of the gut.

entities.name: Mangrove rivulus
entities.fact: The mangrove rivulus can live out of water for weeks, breathing through its skin while hiding in damp logs and leaf litter.

entities.name: Paradise fish
entities.fact: The paradise fish breathes air with a labyrinth organ and was one of the first tropical fish kept in home aquariums.

entities.name: Marbled lungfish
entities.fact: The marbled lungfish breathes air with paired lungs and has one of the largest genomes known, roughly 40 times the size of a human's.

entities.name: Giant snakehead
entities.fact: The giant snakehead breathes air and can grow to more than a metre long, and the parents aggressively guard their bright red young.

entities.name: Kissing gourami
entities.fact: Kissing gouramis press their lips together in a test of strength, and like other gouramis they breathe air with a labyrinth organ.

entities.name: Silver arowana
entities.fact: The silver arowana of the Amazon can breathe air with its swim bladder, and the male broods the eggs in his mouth.

entities.name: Electric eel
entities.fact: The electric eel takes about 80 per cent of its oxygen from the air and must surface to breathe every few minutes.

entities.name: Sea star
entities.fact: Sea stars have no brain or blood, pumping seawater through their bodies to move hundreds of tiny tube feet.

entities.name: Crab
entities.fact: Crabs are found in nearly every tide pool, where they scavenge and hide under rocks as the tide goes out.

entities.name: Sea anemone
entities.fact: A sea anemone is an animal, not a plant; it stings small prey with its tentacles and shelters clownfish that are immune to its sting.

entities.name: Mussel
entities.fact: Mussels anchor themselves to rocks with tough byssus threads and filter plankton from the water flowing over them.

entities.name: Hermit crab
entities.fact: Hermit crabs live in empty snail shells, and some species plant stinging sea anemones on the shell as bodyguards, moving them to each new home.

entities.name: Sea urchin
entities.fact: Sea urchins scrape algae from tide pool rocks with a five-toothed mouth known as Aristotle's lantern.

entities.name: Barnacle
entities.fact: A barnacle is a crustacean related to crabs that glues its head to a rock and kicks food into its mouth with its feathery legs.

entities.name: Limpet
entities.fact: A limpet clamps its cone-shaped shell to the rock at low tide and often returns to the exact same spot, called its home scar.

entities.name: Octopus
entities.fact: Small octopuses hunt crabs in tide pools and can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak.

entities.name: Periwinkle
entities.fact: Periwinkles are small sea snails that graze algae on the rocks and seal their shell with a trapdoor at low tide.

entities.name: Sea snail
entities.fact: Sea snails crawl across tide pool rocks on a single muscular foot, scraping algae with a ribbon of tiny teeth called a radula.

entities.name: Shore crab
entities.fact: The shore crab is one of the most common crabs in European rock pools and has become an invasive species on other coasts around the world.

entities.name: Chiton
entities.fact: A chiton is a mollusc with eight overlapping shell plates that let it curl up like a woodlouse when prised off a rock.

entities.name: Sea cucumber
entities.fact: Some sea cucumbers defend themselves by expelling sticky threads or even their own internal organs, which later regrow.

entities.name: Shrimp
entities.fact: Small shrimps shelter in tide pools and are nearly transparent, which helps them hide from the fish and birds that hunt them.

entities.name: Nudibranch
entities.fact: Nudibranchs are sea slugs, and some steal the stinging cells from the anemones they eat and reuse them for their own defence.

entities.name: Tidepool sculpin
entities.fact: The tidepool sculpin is a small camouflaged fish that can find its way back to its home pool after being carried to another one.

entities.name: Blenny
entities.fact: Blennies are small scaleless fish that wedge themselves into cracks in rock pools, and some can hop between pools over wet rock.

entities.name: Goby
entities.fact: Gobies are tiny bottom-living fish whose pelvic fins are fused into a sucker that holds them onto rocks in surging water.

entities.name: Brittle star
entities.fact: Brittle stars hide under tide pool rocks by day and will shed an arm to escape a predator, regrowing it later.

entities.name: Ochre sea star
entities.fact: The ochre sea star comes in purple or orange and is a keystone predator that stops mussels from taking over the rocky shore.

entities.name: Purple sea urchin
entities.fact: Purple sea urchins can bore shallow pits into solid rock and, left unchecked, can mow down whole kelp forests.

entities.name: Gooseneck barnacle
entities.fact: Gooseneck barnacles cling to wave-battered rocks on a rubbery stalk and are a prized delicacy in Spain and Portugal.

entities.name: Dog whelk
entities.fact: The dog whelk drills through the shells of mussels and barnacles with its tongue-like radula and was once used to make purple dye.

entities.name: Sponge
entities.fact: Sponges are the simplest animals and feed by pumping seawater through thousands of tiny pores, filtering out bacteria and other particles.

entities.name: Sea squirt
entities.fact: A sea squirt starts life as a swimming tadpole-like larva, then glues itself to a rock and spends the rest of its life pumping water through its body to filter food.

entities.name: Sea slater
entities.fact: The sea slater is a large woodlouse of the splash zone that hides in crevices by day and scavenges over the rocks at night.

entities.name: Giant green anemone
entities.fact: The giant green anemone of the Pacific coast gets its colour partly from algae living in its tissues and can grow to about 30 centimetres across.

entities.name: Aggregating anemone
entities.fact: Aggregating anemones clone themselves by splitting in two, forming dense carpets where rival clone armies fight along their borders.

entities.name: Black turban snail
entities.fact: The black turban snail is a common grazer of Pacific tide pools whose empty shells are favourite homes for hermit crabs.

entities.name: Clingfish
entities.fact: The northern clingfish grips wet, slimy rock with a suction disc on its belly strong enough to hold many times its own weight.

entities.name: Beadlet anemone
entities.fact: The beadlet anemone looks like a blob of red jelly at low tide and fights its neighbours with a ring of blue stinging beads below its tentacles.

entities.name: Sea hare
entities.fact: The sea hare is a large sea slug that squirts a cloud of purple ink when it is disturbed.

entities.name: Gumboot chiton
entities.fact: The gumboot chiton is the largest chiton in the world, a reddish-brown lump up to about 36 centimetres long nicknamed the wandering meatloaf.

entities.name: Sand dollar
entities.fact: A sand dollar is a flattened burrowing sea urchin covered in a velvet of tiny spines, and the five-petal pattern on its shell marks its breathing pores.

entities.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
entities.fact: The crown-of-thorns starfish is covered in venomous spines and eats living coral, and population outbreaks can strip whole reefs.

entities.name: Sunflower star
entities.fact: The sunflower star can have up to 24 arms and a metre-wide span, and was nearly wiped out by sea star wasting disease after 2013.

entities.name: Feather star
entities.fact: Feather stars are crinoids that cling to reefs with tiny claw-like legs and can swim short distances by waving their feathery arms.

entities.name: Basket star
entities.fact: A basket star is a brittle star whose arms branch again and again into a tangled net that it spreads at night to catch plankton.

entities.name: Sea lily
entities.fact: Sea lilies are stalked crinoids that look like flowers but are animals, and they were far more common in ancient seas than they are today.

entities.name: Common starfish
entities.fact: The common starfish of the North Atlantic pries open mussels and pushes its stomach out through its mouth to digest them inside the shell.

entities.name: Heart urchin
entities.fact: The heart urchin, or sea potato, is a burrowing urchin with a heart-shaped shell that lives hidden in sand below the low-tide mark.

entities.name: Blue starfish
entities.fact: The blue starfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is a vivid blue and, like other Linckia stars, can regrow a whole new star from a single severed arm.

entities.name: Chocolate chip sea star
entities.fact: The chocolate chip sea star gets its name from the dark, knobbly spines dotted across its back like chocolate chips.

entities.name: Bat star
entities.fact: The bat star has webbing between its arms like a bat's wing and comes in almost every colour from red to purple to mottled.

entities.name: Sea apple
entities.fact: The sea apple is a brightly coloured sea cucumber that feeds with a crown of tentacles and can release a toxin that kills everything in an aquarium.

entities.name: Red sea urchin
entities.fact: The red sea urchin of the Pacific coast can live for more than 100 years, and its roe is sold as uni in sushi restaurants.

entities.name: Green sea urchin
entities.fact: The green sea urchin lives in cold northern waters of both the Atlantic and the Pacific and is harvested for its roe.

entities.name: Pincushion starfish
entities.fact: The pincushion starfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is so plump and rounded that its five arms are barely visible, making it look like a puffed-up pillow.

entities.name: Slate pencil urchin
entities.fact: The slate pencil urchin has thick, blunt reddish spines that were once used as chalk to write on slates.

entities.name: Common sunstar
entities.fact: The common sunstar has between about 8 and 14 arms ringed in red and white and preys on other starfish.

entities.name: Edible sea urchin
entities.fact: The edible sea urchin is a large pinkish urchin of the north-east Atlantic that grazes kelp and is harvested for its roe.

entities.name: Long-spined sea urchin
entities.fact: The mass die-off of long-spined sea urchins in the Caribbean in 1983 let algae overgrow many reefs, showing how important their grazing was.

entities.name: Flower urchin
entities.fact: The flower urchin is one of the most venomous sea urchins, with flower-like pincers that can deliver a painful and occasionally dangerous sting.

entities.name: Sea daisy
entities.fact: Sea daisies are tiny disc-shaped echinoderms found on sunken wood in the deep sea and were only discovered in 1986.

entities.name: Leather star
entities.fact: The leather star has a smooth, leathery skin and is said to smell of garlic when it is lifted from the water.

entities.name: Blood star
entities.fact: The blood star is a small, slender sea star of rocky northern shores, usually a vivid orange-red, with arms much longer than its body is wide.

entities.name: Japanese sea cucumber
entities.fact: The Japanese sea cucumber is farmed and dried as a luxury food across East Asia and is known in Japan as namako.

entities.name: Sea biscuit
entities.fact: A sea biscuit is a thick, domed relative of the sand dollar that burrows through sand on tropical sea floors.

entities.name: Spiny starfish
entities.fact: The spiny starfish of European coasts can reach about 70 centimetres across and is armed with rows of blunt spines ringed by tiny pincers.

entities.name: Sea pig
entities.fact: Sea pigs are plump pink sea cucumbers that trundle across deep abyssal mud on stubby tube-foot legs, sometimes in herds of hundreds.

entities.name: Whale shark
entities.fact: The whale shark is the largest fish in the sea and feeds by filtering plankton and small fish through its sieve-like gill pads.

entities.name: Blue whale
entities.fact: The blue whale, the largest animal ever known, feeds almost entirely on krill, straining it from the water through plates of baleen.

entities.name: Oyster
entities.fact: A single oyster can filter about 190 litres of seawater a day, which is why oyster reefs help keep coastal water clear.

entities.name: Clam
entities.fact: Clams draw seawater in through one siphon, strain out plankton with their gills, and pump it out through the other.

entities.name: Basking shark
entities.fact: The basking shark is the second-largest fish and cruises with its enormous mouth open, straining plankton through its gill rakers.

entities.name: Manta ray
entities.fact: Manta rays funnel plankton into their mouths with two paddle-like lobes on their heads and filter it out with their gill plates.

entities.name: Humpback whale
entities.fact: Humpback whales blow curtains of bubbles to herd fish into a tight ball, then lunge through it with mouths open and strain the catch through baleen.

entities.name: Krill
entities.fact: Antarctic krill filter microscopic algae from the water with a basket of bristled legs and are the main food of blue whales.

entities.name: Scallop
entities.fact: Scallops filter plankton from the water and can swim away from a starfish by clapping their two shells together.

entities.name: Baleen whale
entities.fact: Baleen whales have no teeth; instead they strain krill and small fish from mouthfuls of water through fringed plates of baleen.

entities.name: Right whale
entities.fact: Right whales skim-feed, cruising slowly with their mouths open so that copepods are strained continuously through their long baleen plates.

entities.name: Herring
entities.fact: Herring feed on plankton, filtering it through fine gill rakers, and gather in schools that can number in the millions.

entities.name: Sardine
entities.fact: Sardines strain tiny plankton from the water with their gill rakers and form huge shoals, like the famous sardine run off South Africa.

entities.name: Anchovy
entities.fact: Anchovies swim with their mouths wide open to sieve plankton with their gill rakers, and the Peruvian anchoveta is the most heavily fished species on Earth.

entities.name: Megamouth shark
entities.fact: The megamouth shark was unknown to science until 1976 and filters plankton with a huge mouth that may be lined with light-reflecting tissue.

entities.name: Bowhead whale
entities.fact: The bowhead whale has the longest baleen of any whale, up to about 4 metres, and can live for more than 200 years.

entities.name: Fin whale
entities.fact: The fin whale is the second-largest animal on Earth and lunges through schools of krill and fish, filtering them through its baleen.

entities.name: Grey whale
entities.fact: Grey whales feed unlike any other whale, rolling on their sides to suck up mouthfuls of mud and straining out tiny amphipods through their baleen.

entities.name: Minke whale
entities.fact: The minke whale is the smallest of the rorqual whales and gulps schools of krill and small fish, straining them through its baleen.

entities.name: Feather duster worm
entities.fact: A feather duster worm lives in a tube and spreads a crown of feathery tentacles to filter plankton, snapping back inside at the slightest shadow.

entities.name: Cockle
entities.fact: Cockles live just under the surface of sand and mud, filtering plankton through short siphons, and can jump by flicking their muscular foot.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck is a huge burrowing clam of the Pacific Northwest with a siphon up to a metre long, and it can live for more than 150 years.

entities.name: Salp
entities.fact: Salps are barrel-shaped jelly animals that pump water through their bodies to filter plankton, and they can form chains many metres long.

entities.name: Larvacean
entities.fact: A larvacean is a tiny tadpole-shaped animal that builds a disposable mucus house to filter food, discarding it and building a new one every day or so.

entities.name: Bryozoan
entities.fact: Bryozoans, or moss animals, are colonies of tiny filter feeders that form crusts and fronds, each individual catching food with a ring of tentacles.

entities.name: Lamp shell
entities.fact: Lamp shells look like clams but belong to a separate ancient group, the brachiopods, and filter food with a coiled, tentacled organ called the lophophore.

entities.name: Menhaden
entities.fact: Menhaden are oily filter-feeding fish of the American Atlantic coast, caught in huge numbers for fish oil and fish meal.

entities.name: Giant clam
entities.fact: The giant clam can weigh more than 200 kilograms and feeds both by filtering plankton and on sugars made by algae living in its mantle.

entities.name: Mole crab
entities.fact: Mole crabs burrow backwards into the sand of surf beaches and filter food from the receding waves with their feathery antennae.

entities.name: Christmas tree worm
entities.fact: Christmas tree worms bore into living coral and unfurl two spiral crowns of tentacles to filter plankton, vanishing into their tubes when startled.

entities.name: Pyrosome
entities.fact: A pyrosome is a glowing hollow tube made of thousands of tiny filter-feeding animals that can grow several metres long and is nicknamed the sea pickle.

entities.name: Clownfish
entities.fact: Clownfish are immune to the stings of their host anemone, and if the female of a group dies the largest male changes sex to take her place.

entities.name: Parrotfish
entities.fact: Parrotfish grind coral with beak-like teeth and excrete the remains as fine white sand, producing much of the sand on tropical beaches.

entities.name: Angelfish
entities.fact: Marine angelfish are among the most colourful reef fish, and many change their pattern completely as they grow from juvenile to adult.

entities.name: Blue tang
entities.fact: The blue tang, the fish behind Dory, has a razor-sharp spine on each side of its tail that it flicks out in defence.

entities.name: Butterflyfish
entities.fact: Butterflyfish are thin, bright reef fish that often pair for life and use their pointed snouts to pick at coral polyps.

entities.name: Lionfish
entities.fact: The lionfish defends itself with venomous spines and, released into the Atlantic, has become one of the most damaging invasive reef fish.

entities.name: Moray eel
entities.fact: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throat that shoots forward to drag prey down the gullet.

entities.name: Grouper
entities.fact: Groupers are big-mouthed reef predators that suck in prey whole, and some species have been seen hunting together with moray eels.

entities.name: Wrasse
entities.fact: Wrasses are a huge family of reef fish, many of which start life as females and later change into brightly coloured males.

entities.name: Damselfish
entities.fact: Damselfish are small, feisty reef fish; some farm patches of algae on the reef and chase off intruders many times their size.

entities.name: Triggerfish
entities.fact: A triggerfish locks itself into a crevice at night by raising a dorsal spine that can only be released by a second, smaller trigger spine.

entities.name: Pufferfish
entities.fact: Pufferfish inflate into a spiky ball by gulping water, and many carry tetrodotoxin, a poison far deadlier than cyanide.

entities.name: Seahorse
entities.fact: Seahorses are reef fish that swim upright, grip coral with their tails, and leave the males to carry the eggs in a pouch.

entities.name: Barracuda
entities.fact: The great barracuda is a torpedo-shaped reef predator with fang-like teeth that hunts in sudden short bursts of speed.

entities.name: Snapper
entities.fact: Snappers are schooling reef predators prized as food fish, and the red snapper can live for more than 50 years.

entities.name: Surgeonfish
entities.fact: Surgeonfish are named for the scalpel-like spines at the base of the tail, and they graze algae that would otherwise smother coral.

entities.name: Moorish idol
entities.fact: The Moorish idol, with its long trailing dorsal fin, is notoriously hard to keep in aquariums because it feeds mainly on sponges.

entities.name: Napoleon wrasse
entities.fact: The Napoleon wrasse can grow to about 2 metres long and is one of the few fish that eats the toxic crown-of-thorns starfish.

entities.name: Cardinalfish
entities.fact: Cardinalfish are small nocturnal reef fish, and in most species the male broods the eggs in his mouth without eating until they hatch.

entities.name: Hawkfish
entities.fact: Hawkfish perch on coral heads using their thick pectoral fins, watching for prey like a hawk before darting out to grab it.

entities.name: Squirrelfish
entities.fact: Squirrelfish are red, big-eyed reef fish that hide in caves by day and come out to hunt at night.

entities.name: Boxfish
entities.fact: Boxfish are encased in a rigid box-shaped shell of fused scales, and some release a toxin into the water when stressed.

entities.name: Trumpetfish
entities.fact: The trumpetfish hangs vertically among sea fans and shadows larger fish to sneak up on its prey.

entities.name: Sweetlips
entities.fact: Sweetlips are reef fish named for their thick, fleshy lips, and their juveniles often look nothing like the adults.

entities.name: Anthias
entities.fact: Anthias are the small orange fish that shimmer in clouds above Indo-Pacific reefs, each male guarding a harem of females.

entities.name: Mandarinfish
entities.fact: The mandarinfish is one of only two vertebrates known to make a true blue pigment, and it has no scales but a bitter, toxic coating.

entities.name: Royal gramma
entities.fact: The royal gramma, or fairy basslet, is a purple-and-yellow Caribbean reef fish that often swims upside down beneath ledges.

entities.name: Bumphead parrotfish
entities.fact: The bumphead parrotfish is the largest parrotfish, reaching about 1.3 metres, and rams its forehead into coral to break it up for feeding.

entities.name: Garden eel
entities.fact: Garden eels live in colonies, each anchored tail-first in its own sand burrow, swaying like grass as they pick plankton from the current.

entities.name: Ribbon eel
entities.fact: The ribbon eel starts life black, turns blue as a male and finally yellow as a female.

entities.name: Frogfish
entities.fact: Frogfish are lumpy, camouflaged anglerfish of the reef that lure prey with a fleshy rod on their head and walk on their fins.

entities.name: Dottyback
entities.fact: Dottybacks are small, often vividly coloured reef fish that lurk in crevices, and the orchid dottyback is bred in captivity for aquariums.

entities.name: Whitetip reef shark
entities.fact: The whitetip reef shark is a slender shark that rests in caves on the reef by day and can pump water over its gills without swimming.

entities.name: Brain coral
entities.fact: Brain coral grows into a dome furrowed with grooves like a human brain, and single colonies can live for centuries.

entities.name: Staghorn coral
entities.fact: Staghorn coral grows fast in antler-like branches, but Caribbean staghorn has declined by more than 90 per cent since the 1980s.

entities.name: Sea fan
entities.fact: A sea fan is a soft coral whose colony grows into a flat, lacy fan held side-on to the current to catch drifting plankton.

entities.name: Elkhorn coral
entities.fact: Elkhorn coral's thick branches once built the shallow crests of Caribbean reefs, and it was among the first corals listed as threatened in the United States.

entities.name: Fire coral
entities.fact: Fire coral is not a true coral but a hydrozoan relative of jellyfish, and brushing against it causes a burning sting.

entities.name: Black coral
entities.fact: Black coral has a dark, flexible skeleton that has been carved into jewellery, and some colonies are more than 4,000 years old.

entities.name: Red coral
entities.fact: Red coral from the Mediterranean has been harvested for jewellery for thousands of years and grows only a few millimetres a year.

entities.name: Table coral
entities.fact: Table coral grows outward in broad, flat plates that shade the reef below and give small fish a roof to hide under.

entities.name: Pillar coral
entities.fact: Pillar coral grows in tall columns up to about 3 metres high and, unlike most corals, extends its feeding polyps by day.

entities.name: Star coral
entities.fact: Star corals build the massive boulders of Caribbean reefs, and their polyps leave star-shaped cups in the skeleton.

entities.name: Soft coral
entities.fact: Soft corals have no hard skeleton and sway in the current, supported by tiny limestone needles in their flesh.

entities.name: Stony coral
entities.fact: Stony corals are the reef builders, each polyp laying down a cup of limestone so that colonies slowly pile up into reefs.

entities.name: Mushroom coral
entities.fact: Mushroom corals are single large polyps that live unattached on the sea floor and can creep slowly across the sand.

entities.name: Lettuce coral
entities.fact: Lettuce coral grows in thin, ruffled plates like the leaves of a lettuce and is common on Caribbean reef slopes.

entities.name: Bubble coral
entities.fact: Bubble coral inflates grape-like bladders by day to catch sunlight for its algae and withdraws them at night to feed with its tentacles.

entities.name: Finger coral
entities.fact: Finger coral grows in stubby, finger-like branches and is a sturdy, common coral in the shallows of Caribbean and Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Acropora
entities.fact: Acropora is the largest genus of reef-building corals, including the staghorn and table corals, and is among the first to bleach when the water warms.

entities.name: Porites
entities.fact: Porites corals grow in massive domes so slowly and steadily that scientists drill cores from them to read centuries of ocean climate.

entities.name: Montipora
entities.fact: Montipora corals grow as plates, crusts and branches and are popular in reef aquariums for their bright colours.

entities.name: Sea whip
entities.fact: A sea whip is a soft coral that grows as a single long, flexible rod, often brightly coloured, swaying in the current.

entities.name: Organ pipe coral
entities.fact: Organ pipe coral has a bright red skeleton of parallel tubes like organ pipes, hidden under greyish-green polyps.

entities.name: Blue coral
entities.fact: Blue coral is the only living coral with a blue skeleton, coloured by iron salts, and is the sole survivor of an ancient group.

entities.name: Cauliflower coral
entities.fact: Cauliflower coral grows in knobbly clumps and is one of the first corals to settle on new reef, but also one of the first to bleach.

entities.name: Leather coral
entities.fact: Leather corals are soft corals shaped like a toadstool with a leathery surface, and they shed a waxy film to clean themselves.

entities.name: Gorgonian
entities.fact: Gorgonians are soft corals with a flexible, horn-like skeleton, growing as sea fans, whips and bushes.

entities.name: Lophelia
entities.fact: Lophelia is a cold-water coral that builds reefs in the dark, hundreds of metres down, from Norway to the Gulf of Mexico.

entities.name: Bamboo coral
entities.fact: Bamboo corals of the deep sea have skeletons of limestone segments joined by dark, flexible nodes, like a bamboo stem.

entities.name: Torch coral
entities.fact: Torch coral has long, flowing tentacles tipped with glowing knobs and is a favourite of reef aquarists.

entities.name: Hammer coral
entities.fact: Hammer coral's tentacles end in hammer or anchor-shaped tips, and it sends out long sweeper tentacles to sting neighbouring corals.

entities.name: Frogspawn coral
entities.fact: Frogspawn coral is named for its bubbly tentacle tips, which look like a mass of frog's eggs.

entities.name: Sun coral
entities.fact: Sun coral has no symbiotic algae, so it can grow in dark caves and under piers, opening its bright orange polyps at night to catch plankton.

entities.name: Carnation coral
entities.fact: Carnation corals are soft corals that puff up into brilliant pink, red and purple bushes at night and collapse into limp blobs by day.

entities.name: Bubblegum coral
entities.fact: Bubblegum coral is a deep-sea soft coral that grows into pink, tree-like colonies up to several metres tall, with branch tips like blobs of chewed gum.

entities.name: Remora
entities.fact: Remoras hitch rides on sharks, whales, turtles and even ships using a suction disc on top of the head, eating scraps and parasites.

entities.name: Cleaner wrasse
entities.fact: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse runs a cleaning station where bigger fish queue to have parasites picked from their skin, gills and even mouths.

entities.name: Cleaner shrimp
entities.fact: Cleaner shrimp wave their white antennae to advertise, then climb onto fish, and even into the mouths of moray eels, to pick off parasites.

entities.name: Pilot fish
entities.fact: Pilot fish swim alongside sharks, rays and turtles, feeding on scraps and parasites, and are rarely attacked by their hosts.

entities.name: Pearlfish
entities.fact: The pearlfish spends the day hiding inside the body of a sea cucumber, slipping in tail-first through its anus.

entities.name: Pistol shrimp
entities.fact: The pistol shrimp digs a burrow it shares with a goby; the nearly blind shrimp keeps one antenna on the fish, which flicks its tail to warn of danger.

entities.name: Shrimp goby
entities.fact: Shrimp gobies stand guard at the mouth of a burrow dug by a pistol shrimp, warning the shrimp with a flick of the tail when danger approaches.

entities.name: Whale barnacle
entities.fact: Whale barnacles grow embedded in the skin of humpback and grey whales, riding along for a free supply of plankton-rich water.

entities.name: Pea crab
entities.fact: The pea crab is a tiny soft-shelled crab that lives inside the shell of a living oyster or mussel, stealing food from its host's gills.

entities.name: Anemone shrimp
entities.fact: Anemone shrimps are nearly transparent and live unharmed among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, sometimes cleaning passing fish.

entities.name: Boxer crab
entities.fact: The boxer crab holds a tiny stinging sea anemone in each claw like a pair of pom-poms and waves them at anything that threatens it.

entities.name: Tongue-eating louse
entities.fact: The tongue-eating louse is an isopod that enters a fish through its gills, drains the blood from its tongue, and then takes the tongue's place.

entities.name: Whale louse
entities.fact: Whale lice are not lice but crustaceans that cling to the skin folds and rough patches of whales, especially right whales.

entities.name: Decorator crab
entities.fact: Decorator crabs snip off bits of sponge, seaweed and even small anemones and hook them onto their shells as living camouflage.

entities.name: Anemone porcelain crab
entities.fact: The spotted porcelain crab lives among the tentacles of large sea anemones, filtering plankton from the water with its feathery mouthparts.

entities.name: Sea louse
entities.fact: Sea lice are tiny copepods that attach to salmon and feed on their skin and blood, and they are a major problem on salmon farms.

entities.name: Coral goby
entities.fact: Coral gobies are tiny fish that live their whole lives among the branches of a single Acropora coral colony, which they defend from seaweed.

entities.name: Emperor shrimp
entities.fact: The emperor shrimp rides on sea cucumbers and large nudibranchs, cleaning its host and hitching a lift across the sea floor.

entities.name: Domino damselfish
entities.fact: Young domino damselfish shelter among the tentacles of sea anemones, like clownfish, before moving onto coral heads as adults.

entities.name: Turtle barnacle
entities.fact: Turtle barnacles settle on the shells of sea turtles and ride with them, filtering food from the water as the turtle swims.

entities.name: Crinoid shrimp
entities.fact: Crinoid shrimps live hidden among the arms of feather stars and match their host's colours exactly, from yellow to black.

entities.name: Whip coral goby
entities.fact: The whip coral goby is a tiny fish that spends its whole life clinging to a single strand of whip coral.

entities.name: Sponge crab
entities.fact: Sponge crabs cut a living sponge to size and hold it over their backs with their hind legs as a disguise, and the sponge keeps on growing.

entities.name: Zebra urchin crab
entities.fact: The zebra crab lives among the spines of sea urchins, where its bold black and white stripes hide it from predators.

entities.name: Coleman shrimp
entities.fact: Coleman shrimps live in pairs on the venomous fire urchin, clearing a patch of spines to sit among its brilliant colours.

entities.name: Crinoid squat lobster
entities.fact: The crinoid squat lobster lives among the arms of feather stars, striped to match its host.

entities.name: Gall crab
entities.fact: Gall crabs settle on living coral as larvae and let the coral grow around them, sealing the female inside a chamber for life.

entities.name: Man-of-war fish
entities.fact: The man-of-war fish lives among the deadly tentacles of the Portuguese man o' war, nibbling on them while sheltering from predators.
